newsitem.title: SPAIN: FORECAST- Spain's Jan CPI expected to fall to 3%.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST- Spain's Jan CPI expected to fall to 3%.

text.p: Spanish inflation should start the new year on an old downtrend, with January data seen approaching three percent versus 3.2 percent in December, analysts said on Tuesday.
A Reuter poll forecast the increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) to be a monthly 0.42 percent, a 3.0 percent year-on-year rise.
This compares with 0.3 pct and 3.2 pct respectively in December. January CPI is due on Thursday, February 13.

Many factors, from a lower trend in fresh food prices to modest increases in regulated tariffs, are thought behind the downtrend, and analysts expect Spanish inflation to continue its fall for the whole of the first half of 1997.

"We think (January) CPI, on monthly basis, could be around 0.3 percent, which will bring the year-on-year rate to 2.9 percent both in the general and core indices," said Carmen Hernansanz, economist at Merrill Lynch in Madrid.
Core inflation excludes energy and fresh food prices.
She added that fresh food should have risen less than during last January, similar to oil and energy prices.
In January 1996, inflation rose 0.6 percent month-on-month.
Salomon Brothers in London is expecting the CPI to rise around 3.0 percent year-on-year, with less volatile core inflation at around 2.8 percent year-on-year.

"What we are seeing is a continuation of the declining trend. We'll have a fall in the core rate and in fresh food which won't be compensated by rising energy prices," said Riccardo Barbieri, economist at Morgan Stanley in London.
Spanish inflation is expected to decline steadily in the first five months of this year, particularly because of favourable comparison with last year's high rates.

"We expect inflation to slip steadily until somewhere above 2.0 percent in May, and then from there it should recover to end the year at around 2.7 percent, averaging 3.0 percent in 1998" said Antoni Espasa, director of the independent economists group in Madrid which publishes in inflation bulletin.
While this year the inflation rate could see the benefit of positive comparisons versus 1996 in many items, this will not be true for olive oil or meat in 1998, Espasa added.
Earlier today, the Bank of Spain's latest report said the slowdown in services prices may have bottomed out while energy prices may be picking up.
Overall, official forecasts point to inflation of around 2.5/2.7 percent in December 1997.
